name: Automation

claims.claim_text: Electronics assembly crossed an economic threshold: where the cheap route was once hand-stuffing boards wherever labour was cheapest, buying even a low-end pick-and-place machine became both faster and cheaper than that.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's faster and more cost-effective to buy, you know, even just a low-end pick-and-place machine
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: The work does not vanish when a machine takes over, it moves. Loading a placement machine requires organisation, a stock room and continuous attention to keep the equipment running, so a substantial amount of labour surrounds the automated step.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not like it's easy to load up a pick-and-place
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: A second-order effect runs the other way from the usual story: the facility needed to house automated assembly equipment must be of a higher standard than a hand-assembly shop, so working conditions can improve even as headcount falls.
claims.quote_verbatim: the facilities you need to put these pick-and-place machines in generally are of a higher standard
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Where a process stays manual it is usually about cost rather than capability. If people can be found to do it cheaply enough there is no incentive to invest, so the presence of manual labour is evidence about wages rather than about technical difficulty.
claims.quote_verbatim: there has to be a financial incentive to do it
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Specific stages resist automation for physical reasons: parts that cannot pass through a water wash, masking operations, and anything requiring high dexterity. These are the points where a human is still in the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's different steps of the process where sometimes it's just you need human labor
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Wiring harnesses remain substantially hand-made, built on large peg boards where an operator loops the wires by hand. There is automation around the process, but the first build of a new harness is where the difficulty concentrates.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use these loops to make the wiring harnesses

claims.claim_text: The decision to automate is arithmetic rather than ideology: count the shifts, the workers on each, the hours and the wage, and compare the total against the cost of the equipment until a balance point appears.
claims.quote_verbatim: eventually you start to find some balance point where you're like, oh, we should just put a robot in

claims.claim_text: The technology is rarely the constraint. Industrial arms have been available for decades, so what changes when a factory automates is the economic balance rather than what is possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not even the technology availability

claims.claim_text: Published figures from automated plants are rare because companies keep them internal, which makes the occasional disclosed set worth noting: ninety percent of the workforce replaced, production up by 250 percent and defects down by eighty.
claims.quote_verbatim: 90% production rises by 250. Defects drop by 80

claims.claim_text: Any competent operation measures the efficiency of an automation project against what preceded it, precisely to confirm the investment came out ahead. The absence of such measurement is itself a warning sign.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they automate something, they measure the efficiency of that

claims.claim_text: The self-assembly threshold sits around a hundred units. Below it, assembling in-house can make sense for someone under schedule pressure; above it, going to a contract manufacturer is the answer unless there is a specific financial reason not to.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you get above 100, you know, like why?

claims.claim_text: What makes in-house assembly work at that scale is constraining the design to the process: using only parts already loaded in your own machine and building up scripts over years, so the whole flow is optimised around one setup.
claims.quote_verbatim: He only uses parts that he knows are in his pick and place machine

claims.claim_text: The human limit on repetitive kitting work is about a hundred units in one sitting before eyes and hands start to degrade. Two or three hundred over a weekend leaves the person wiped out, which is the practical reason such work gets automated first.
claims.quote_verbatim: A hundred is about as many as I would want to do in one sitting
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: What separates well-run assembly shops is thinking about the whole flow rather than the machine. The good ones decide in advance how a new machine will be fed and unloaded and buy the automation around it rather than just the machine itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: they wouldn't just buy a machine, but they would buy all the automation around the machine
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A concrete measure of how rare that thinking is: across roughly a hundred contract manufacturers and original equipment makers visited, only fifteen or twenty had anything other than a table or a cardboard ramp catching boards coming out of the reflow oven.
claims.quote_verbatim: besides a table or a cardboard ramp catching circuit boards out of the reflow oven
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The visible sign of a well-run shop is machines running with nobody standing in front of them, because the underlying economics are that machines are cheap and people are expensive. People manually loading and unloading equipment all day is the opposite signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: machines aren't expensive. People are expensive
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Automation pays at small batch sizes too, and does not require huge runs. A buffer holding fifteen boards ahead of a machine and an unloader holding fifteen after it lets an operator start the job and leave, which is the whole benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to have a buffer before this machine with 15 boards
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The stubborn manual step in assembly automation is new component data. An unfamiliar part still requires a person to find the datasheet and determine its dimensions before the machine can handle it, and that problem is not solved.
claims.quote_verbatim: it still requires you looking up a data sheet and determining what size that component is
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The larger cumulative gains are in unglamorous places rather than on the production floor: receiving, shipping and clerical steps such as putting an order onto the schedule. Each may take only thirty seconds, and eliminating many of them compounds.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe it only took 30 seconds, but now you don't have to do it anymore
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Programming boards during assembly has a quantity threshold. At around fifty boards it does not pay; at five hundred it does, because the setup can be automated. Parts arriving pre-programmed from the supplier is better than either.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's just, you know, maybe 50 boards, it's just, doesn't really make sense
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: On a benchtop placement machine the fully automated case is 8 and 12 millimetre tape, with wider tapes handled from strip or tray. Which board suits the machine matters less than why the boards are needed, since that determines the acceptable degree of manual intervention.
claims.quote_verbatim: mostly an eight and 12 is super home run
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: A widely cited correction came from a heavily automated vehicle line whose own founder concluded that excessive automation had been a mistake and that humans were underrated. It is the most prominent public reversal on the subject.
claims.quote_verbatim: excessive automation at Tesla was a mistake

claims.claim_text: The mechanism behind that reversal is inflexibility. Reconfigurable robots do not really exist yet at large manufacturing scale, so tooling up a precisely automated process while the product is still changing locks you into decisions you need to revisit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole idea of, of reconfigurable robots is still not there

claims.claim_text: The cost assumption is also frequently wrong. Industrial robots are plausibly more expensive than the humans they replace, so automation is not automatically the cheap option and the case has to be made per application.
claims.quote_verbatim: robots are probably more expensive than humans
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The trajectory of machine design runs from custom toward general: most machines are bespoke now, more dexterous general-purpose arms will generalise and fall in price, and they will then be integrated more widely. The limit is that a custom machine still beats a general one at its own task.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't beat custom machines to do stuff

claims.claim_text: Lowering the barrier to building automation gives access to precision that changes what can be built at all. A custom coil-winding machine assembled in about two hours produced identical coils every time, which hand winding could not.
claims.quote_verbatim: lowering the barrier of entry for automation so that you have access to more precision
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: The automation that actually displaces electronics designers is not automated design tools. It is silicon integration: chip companies absorbing more functions onto the die to capture more of the system, which removes the design work rather than performing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: chip companies want to make more money and grab more of the market
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: The visible consequence is that following an application note gets a newcomer capability that used to need a team, with high-speed interfaces working on a two-layer board provided the connector is close enough to the chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: any schmuck can come along and follow the application note circuit
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Nobody objects while this happens because each step is beneficial: products get built faster and more becomes possible. The displacement is real but invisible in the moment, which is what makes it hard to reason about.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one's going to complain about it because it's beneficial
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Automation wins eventually in any task where it is suitable, because equipment can run effectively around the clock. The interesting questions are only when, and which tasks go first.
claims.quote_verbatim: automation will always win out eventually. It's just a matter of when and which tasks go first
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: The most exposed work is not the visible service jobs people imagine but long-haul driving and document-heavy professional work, where the task is well defined and the volume is large.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be the, the long haul trucks driver stuff
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: On the attribution question, most manufacturing jobs that disappeared went to automation rather than to offshoring, which is a different diagnosis with different consequences from the one usually offered.
claims.quote_verbatim: Most of those jobs are actually lost to automation
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: Long-distance haulage is a strong automation candidate for structural reasons: the vehicle can run continuously without rest, and much of the driving already happens at night when conditions are simplest.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can just keep driving all day, all night

claims.claim_text: There is a wage mechanism separate from job losses. As machines take over more of a task, the residual human skill becomes less specialised, which puts downward pressure on the pay of the people still doing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Which means there's more and more downward pressure

claims.claim_text: The transition matters as much as the destination. Automating a process that people currently perform creates dispute in a way that designing full automation from the start does not, so the same end state produces very different friction depending on the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: imagine if they would have started with humans assembling and then eventually they replace it

claims.claim_text: The staged approach to automating a warehouse is to remove the movement first, bringing shelves to a stationary worker, and keep the human for recognising and picking the object. The second stage, replacing the picking itself, is the genuinely hard part.
claims.quote_verbatim: You replace all the stupid parts
claims.episode_title: Compare and Contrast Tech Entitlement - Worldly Working Wonks

claims.claim_text: That decision rests on measurement: timing workers with a stopwatch across many employees to establish an average before concluding that an automated system delivering parts to them would be quicker.
claims.quote_verbatim: timing how long it takes on, on average
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Compare and Contrast Tech Entitlement - Worldly Working Wonks

claims.claim_text: The strongest counter-argument to automating everything is that the simple version is often better. A light switch will always be simpler, cheaper and more reliable than any automation system that replaces it, and that comparison does not change with technology.
claims.quote_verbatim: a light switch will always, always be better, simpler, cheaper, more reliable than any automation system

claims.claim_text: The rebuttal is that such comparisons reason from the systems we already know. The real opportunity in a domain is usually something the current framing cannot see, in the way that a paper-reel calculator argument does not anticipate what a computer becomes useful for.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're thinking in terms of light switches

claims.claim_text: The dividing line is universality. Where automation is genuinely useful to everyone it wins and doing the task any other way becomes silly; where it is not, people keep the older method because it remains better and simpler for them.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's unavoidable for the things that are genuinely universally useful

claims.claim_text: A defensible personal limit: over-automation costs more effort than it returns, and there is real value in keeping direct manual control of things you actually enjoy controlling.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not into over automation

claims.claim_text: The characteristic failure mode of automation is silence. A process that stops working can go unnoticed for months precisely because its whole purpose was that nobody had to watch it, so anything automated needs its own check that it is still running.
claims.quote_verbatim: It lulls you to sleep

claims.claim_text: The consultant's rule is to automate or buy out everything that is not what your time is for. Payroll, tax filing and bookkeeping through a paid service costs less than the hours it consumes, because those hours are better spent on client work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should use automation when you can
claims.speaker: Jeremiah Gillis

claims.claim_text: Command-line tools remain necessary for automation even as vendors push integrated environments, because scripting a build or a test requires something a graphical interface cannot provide. Their absence closes off the whole approach.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you really want to automate stuff, you really... You need those command line tools

claims.claim_text: Automated testing for hardware follows the software pattern: a script stimulates the board, runs a suite and reports which tests a change has broken. Bench instruments increasingly ship Python libraries, so measurement equipment can be pulled into the same scripts.
claims.quote_verbatim: I ran a hundred tests and Chris, that change you just made broke 40 of them
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: Distributor interfaces lag on the purchasing side. Data access through published interfaces is reasonably established, but ordering programmatically is not, so full procurement automation remains out of reach for now.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm afraid it might take some more time until we get the full automation

claims.claim_text: Laziness in the specific sense of refusing to repeat a manual loop is a virtue in engineering. Automating data acquisition and analysis rather than performing it repeatedly is what makes the measurement work tractable.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm real big on automation because I'm lazy
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: An agricultural monitoring deployment failed on an assumption rather than on technology. Water levels in rice paddies were relayed to a smartphone application, but most of the farmers were older and did not have smartphones, so the automation reached nobody.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the rice farmers are older. They don't have smartphones
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: The argument against removing the human from the loop is not technical: reliability and convenience are bought by giving up the randomness, mistakes and fallibility that come with people, and that trade has consequences worth naming explicitly.
claims.quote_verbatim: we pay for that security that convenience, that reliability by giving up our humanity in the process
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: The engineering counterpoint from spaceflight is redundancy rather than autonomy. The lunar module carried six independent methods of launching if things failed, and every account from the crews stresses backups upon backups.
claims.quote_verbatim: six different backup methods to launch if things failed

claims.claim_text: The reason humans stay in the loop at all is the same reason those backups existed: something goes wrong and a person has to take over. That argument is why training for the manual case remains necessary even in a highly automated system.
claims.quote_verbatim: something's going to go wrong at some point

claims.claim_text: A realistic forecast for robotics is steady expansion rather than explosive growth: no hockey stick comparable to the internet, but continued deployment wherever safety, price, performance and flexibility line up for a given problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think globally we're going to see like a hockey stick growth in robotics
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner

claims.claim_text: The consulting opportunity in robotics is horizontal rather than vertical. Power systems, radios, computing and cameras in a robot are not very different from those elsewhere, so expertise in one of those technologies transfers directly into helping robotics companies reach market sooner.
claims.quote_verbatim: the power systems in these things are not that different from other sorts of power systems

claims.claim_text: The usual outcome of automating menial work is not elimination but a shift up the value chain with wider coverage: someone who checked the water in twenty pools a day becomes the person managing the pools for a region.
claims.quote_verbatim: Now they become the pool manager for a region

claims.claim_text: The disappointment with automation so far is that it removed drudgery without reducing hours. The freed time was absorbed by whatever came next, which is a choice about expectations rather than a property of the technology.
claims.quote_verbatim: we automated the drudgery tasks, but we didn't expect people to work less
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Whoever owns the automation with human intelligence directing it comes out ahead, because the machinery supplies no creativity of its own. That is the argument for being on the building side of automation rather than the displaced side.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because they don't have creativity
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Useful home automation is conditional and retrofitted rather than wholesale: an existing door with a sensor added, plus a rule that closes it if it has been open for twenty minutes, solves a real problem without replacing anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: if the garage door has been open for 20 minutes, trigger it
